My grandma in Cairo was diagnosed with Parkinson's six months ago. I'm studying engineering part-time and I call her every week but lately after we hang up I just cry. She sounds weaker each time and there's nothing I can do from here. I feel so disconnected from her and from my own life.

Hearing someone you love sound weaker each week, and not being able to do anything but listen, is genuinely painful, and crying after those calls makes complete sense. A couple of practical things: ask her doctor's clinic whether there's a local Parkinson's support group or community nurse who could visit, so she has in-person support beyond you. And for yourself, those tears after every call are worth mentioning to your university's student counselling service. You're grieving something real alongside the caregiving. You don't have to hold that alone.

I graduated in history last year and I'm job-hunting in London while caring for my grandma who has chronic pain. She lives with me and it's been about a year. I love her but some days her pain makes her snappy and I take it personally even though I know I shouldn't. Then I feel awful for being hurt.

When someone you love is in pain and becomes snappy, it's natural to feel hurt even when you know the pain is speaking, your emotions don't switch off just because you understand the cause. That doesn't make you unkind. It makes you a person absorbing a hard situation daily. Two things: ask her GP about a pain management referral if she doesn't already have one, because better pain control can ease everyone's experience. And when you're job-hunting, try to carve out time outside the home, a library, a café, so the caregiving environment and your work space aren't the same four walls.

I'm 19, studying history in Madrid. My mum has schizophrenia and I live with her. It's been about six months since her last relapse and she's stable but I'm constantly on alert, checking if she's taking her meds, watching her mood. I can't relax at home. My faith teaches compassion but I'm just so tired of being vigilant.

Living in a state of constant vigilance, checking meds, watching mood, never quite letting your guard down, is exhausting in a way that builds up quietly, and being tired of it doesn't mean you've run out of compassion. It means your nervous system is overstretched. Two things: ask your mum's care team if there's a community mental health nurse or support worker who could do some of the medication monitoring, so it's not solely on you. And look for a carers' support group through your local mental health services, meeting others who live this specific vigilance can ease the loneliness of it. You need home to feel like home too, not a watchtower.

I'm 23, studying psychology in Manila. My older sister has diabetes with complications and I've been helping coordinate her care from a distance for a few months. She keeps skipping meals and not checking her blood sugar. I've tried everything, reminding her, ordering her supplies, talking to her doctor. Nothing works and I feel like I'm failing her.

Watching your sister not manage her health despite everything you're doing, and feeling like her choices reflect on your efforts, is a really painful position, and it's one many carers reach when the person they care for isn't following medical advice. But her choices are hers, not a measure of your care. What would help: is there a diabetes educator or counsellor her doctor could refer her to, someone who works with the emotional side of managing chronic illness, not just the clinical side? And for you: what would it look like to step back from monitoring and let her care team hold that? You can love her without being responsible for every decision she makes.

My aunt in another province has schizophrenia and I've been her long-distance support for over five years. I work part-time in psychology here in the Philippines and I feel like I should be better at this by now. But every crisis still hits me like it's the first time.

Five years in and every crisis still hitting hard isn't a sign you're bad at this. It's a sign you love someone whose illness is unpredictable, and no amount of experience makes that stop hurting. Psychology training teaches you to understand patterns. It doesn't make you immune to the emotional impact. One thing worth trying: after each crisis, note what helped and what didn't, so you're not starting from scratch each time. And if you have a supervisor or mentor in your psychology work, talking through the emotional side of being a caregiver, not just the clinical side, could be valuable. You deserve support too, not just skills.

My grandmother had a stroke about a year ago and lives with me in the Netherlands. I'm studying social work and my Hindu faith is very important to me. It frames seva as my duty. But between physio appointments, medication management, and my studies, I'm running on empty. My temple community helps but I don't ask enough.

Your sense of seva is clearly a deep anchor, and a year of co-resident care alongside full-time study is an enormous amount. Running on empty isn't a failure of duty. It's what happens when one person carries too much. One practical step: pick one person in your temple community and ask for something specific, a meal, a weekly visit, help with transport to an appointment. People want to help. They often just need to be told how. And if your university has a carer support service, use it. Asking for help is part of sustaining seva, not a departure from it.

My grandfather in another city has had a spinal cord injury for over five years now. I'm studying business in Germany and trying to support from here. I feel like I should know by now what help exists but I've never really looked into carer support for myself.

Five years and only now looking into support for yourself is incredibly common. Most carers put themselves last. In Germany, start with the Pflegestützpunkt (care support point) in your grandfather's region. They advise family carers on available services and benefits. Also look into the German Red Cross family caregiver support programs, which offer phone consultation and local groups. You've been carrying this quietly. Reaching out now isn't a failure, it's a smart next step.

My older sibling had a stroke six months ago and lives with me here in Canada. I work full-time in medicine so you'd think I'd know where to get support, but I'm too close to it. I need to find carer support for myself, not more clinical information.

Being a healthcare professional doesn't make you immune to the weight of caring for family, if anything, it can be harder because you know too much. The Canadian Stroke and Recovery Foundation has resources specifically for family carers, and the Young Carers Initiative in Canada may offer peer support for someone your age. Also, your sibling's rehab team can connect you with a social worker who understands family carer burnout. You need space to be a sibling, not just a clinician.

I'm 20, Black Caribbean, Christian (it's very important to me), doing a business apprenticeship in Kenya. My mum has diabetes with complications and I've lived with and cared for her about six months. I'd use online support but I want something that understands faith matters in how I cope, not just 'self-care' talk.

That's a fair thing to want, when faith is central to how you make sense of things, generic self-care language can feel hollow. A few places to look: diabetes organisations with faith-sensitive carer pathways, your church community (some congregations have carer support circles), and Christian carer networks that blend practical caregiving with spiritual grounding. Online, some faith-based carer platforms offer both peer discussion and prayer or reflection alongside practical tips. Would you like help finding which of those might be accessible in Kenya, or would you prefer to start with something international?

I'm in Mexico City studying biology and working part-time. My grandmother lives with us and has bipolar disorder, three years now. All the online resources are either for the person with bipolar or for their parents, not for a granddaughter who's 20 and also trying to get through uni. I can't find anything that fits.

That mismatch is frustrating. Most mental health carer content assumes a parent or spouse, not a grandchild juggling study and work. Try searching 'jóvenes cuidadores salud mental México'. There are emerging young-carer networks in Mexico that specifically address mental health in the family. Also, your university's student support service likely has counselling that can factor in your caregiving context. It's not just for academic stress. One conversation there might open doors you didn't know existed. You shouldn't have to fit yourself into resources designed for someone else's role.

My aunt moved in with us in Lagos about a year ago. She has MS and some days she won't let me help with anything, then other days she's upset I didn't step in. I'm studying engineering and I never know which version of her I'm getting. It's exhausting.

That unpredictability is one of the hardest parts. You're constantly second-guessing and still getting it 'wrong.' MS fatigue and mood changes can fluctuate day to day, so her needs genuinely do shift, which means neither version is the 'real' her. On days she pushes you away, try leaving a neutral offer open: 'I'm here if you need me, no rush.' On days she's upset you didn't help, a simple check-in earlier in the day, 'just checking, do you want a hand today?', can prevent that gap. MS support organisations have good resources on this push-pull dynamic, and her care team can help you read the pattern.

My best friend has cystic fibrosis and I'm studying nursing in Sweden but we're in different cities. He's started pushing me away and cancelling calls. When I ask if something's wrong he says nothing, but I know his health has been worse lately. I pray about it but I also feel useless from here.

It's really hard to be kept at arm's length when you're trying to stay close, and the distance makes everything feel more helpless. Sometimes people pull away when their health worsens because they don't want to be seen differently or feel like a burden. A low-pressure message, something like 'no need to reply, just want you to know I'm here', can keep the door open without demanding energy he may not have. Does he have other people in his daily life who might give you a quiet heads-up if things get serious? And have you been able to talk to him about what he wants from you when things get rough, outside of a crisis moment?

My uncle has a genetic illness and moved in with me in Brazil a few months ago. He's started refusing to let me come to his medical appointments with him, but then he comes back confused about what the doctor said and I can't help properly. I'm an apprentice in psychology and I feel stuck.

That's a really common and frustrating cycle, he wants independence at the appointment but then needs support afterwards, and you're left trying to piece it together. His desire for privacy is understandable, and so is your need to know what's going on to help him. A couple of questions: would he be open to you going but sitting in the waiting room, so he has independence in the room but someone to debrief with straight after? Or would he let him and his doctor record a short summary of key points that you could listen to together at home? Sometimes a middle-ground option respects his autonomy and still gets you the information. Has he said what specifically he doesn't want you to hear?

My grandmother is back in our home country and I'm studying law here in Vietnam. For the past year I've been managing her schizophrenia care remotely, calling clinics, refilling prescriptions, talking her through episodes. I'm Christian and I pray about it but I feel like I should be there and the guilt won't stop.

Managing someone's psychiatric care from another country for a year is real, heavy caregiving, and the guilt of not being physically present is one of the most common and painful parts of distance care. Can I ask: is there anyone locally, a neighbour, a community member from your church, a clinic social worker, who could be your eyes and ears on the ground? Also, what would your grandmother say if she knew you were carrying this much guilt on top of everything you already do? Sometimes the person we're caring for would want us to be gentler with us than we are with ourselves.

And have you and she talked about what 'stable' looks like and what you'd do if things shifted? Knowing that while things are calm can save a lot of scrambling later. Glad you reached out.

My little brother has a genetic illness that's shaped our family for three years now. I'm doing a business apprenticeship in Guadalajara and we live at home. I started meditating with a local Buddhist group which helps me stay calm, but when I come home the calm disappears and I feel guilty that I needed to leave to find it.

That guilt about needing space away to find calm is something many co-resident carers recognise, leaving to recharge can feel like abandoning, even when it's the opposite. A couple of questions: is there a way to bring a small piece of that calm home with you, even five minutes of sitting in your room before re-entering the household? And does your brother or your family know where you go and why, or is it something you keep to yourself? Sometimes naming it simply, 'this helps me come back steadier', removes the guilt for everyone.

And if the distance-ache doesn't ease, a counsellor at your university could help you sit with it.

My best friend has diabetes complications and we've been flatmates for about a year. I'm a med student in Warsaw and I help with his care. My Hindu community is supportive from a distance but I feel like I crossed a line from friend to carer and I don't know how to talk to him about it without hurting him.

That shift from friend to carer is one of the trickiest transitions, and the fact you're worried about hurting him shows how much the friendship matters to you. Two questions: has he ever acknowledged the shift himself, or is it unspoken between you? And are there tasks you're doing that could go to a healthcare professional instead, so you can be his friend first? Sometimes the conversation isn't 'I'm your carer now' but 'I want to make sure I'm being the friend you need, not just the helper.' How do you think he'd respond if you framed it that way?

It's a lot to hold, recovery and job hunting at once. A few starting points: Brazil has organizations like ANDC that support stroke families, and your local municipality may offer home support you can request. If you're job-seeking, some employment programmes give priority to caregivers, worth asking at your local labour office. Also, your synagogue or community centre might know volunteers who could help with transport or meals. You don't have to build this alone from scratch.

Day by day is how everyone starts, and looking for something more structured after six months is a natural next step. A couple of questions: does your grandmother have a regular doctor or clinic that knows her well, and have you asked them what support services they can connect you with? And have you looked into local disability organisations in Jakarta, some offer family carer support or home visit programmes. Also, is there anyone in your family or community who could share even one task a week? Sometimes one small handover creates breathing room you didn't expect.

Running on empty after five years of giving without receiving isn't a personal failure. It's what happens when no one offers you a seat. A couple of questions: have you contacted Macmillan? They support family carers, not just patients, and their helpline can talk you through what's available. And does your grandfather's care team know you're his main long-distance support? Sometimes that triggers a referral to a carer support service. Also, your workplace may have an employee assistance programme, worth checking. You've kept going. Now let something catch you.

I'm a history student in the US and my uncle has cystic fibrosis. I've been supporting him from two hours away for about two years. Being Hindu is part of how I process things, but I'd only join an online group if it were actually useful and not just people venting. I need something structured.

Needing structure rather than open venting is a clear and useful filter, some people process by talking, others by learning, and both are valid. Cystic fibrosis foundations often run structured online education sessions for family members that cover practical management and updates in care, which might suit you better than an open forum. Some also have facilitated peer groups with a set format rather than free discussion. Your uncle's CF clinic may know of family education programs you could join virtually. Structured support exists. It just doesn't always advertise itself as loudly as the informal stuff.

My boyfriend has had long COVID for three years now. I graduated in CS in São Paulo but can't find work, and every online group I find is people sharing miracle cures and supplements. I just want somewhere evidence-based where I won't be told to try magnesium baths.

That frustration is completely valid, long COVID communities have been flooded with unverified remedies, and as someone who's been in this for three years, you need better than that. Look for groups affiliated with post-COVID clinics, university research programmes, or recognised respiratory or rehabilitation organisations. They tend to moderate more strictly. What would actually help you most right now, practical day-to-day management tips, or connecting with other partners who understand the long haul? And have you come across any hospital-based long COVID programmes near him that might have associated patient or family networks?

Can I ask, are you mainly looking for medical information about her condition, or more for emotional and spiritual support for yourself as her grandchild? I live with my cousin who has Down syndrome and I've been his main carer for over five years here in Indonesia. I work full-time in education. Every online support group treats Down syndrome like it's a childhood thing. He's an adult now. I can't find anything about adult caregiving.

You've hit a well-known gap. Down syndrome support is overwhelmingly geared toward parents of children, and adult caregiving resources are much harder to find. Try searching specifically for 'adult Down syndrome' or 'Down syndrome ageing' alongside your country's disability organisations. Some have adult-focused branches that just aren't well advertised. International Down syndrome associations often have adult life sections too. If you tell me roughly where in Indonesia you're based, I can suggest what type of organisation to search for first, and your local disability council may know of adult-focused groups that don't show up easily online.

What are you most looking for, practical day-to-day support, or connection with other long-term carers who understand? All the online support is either crisis-focused or for parents. I'm a partner. I need something about the long-term, day-to-day reality.

What does the day-to-day look like for you, are you mainly managing check-ins and emotional support, or helping coordinate his care from afar? My girlfriend had a traumatic brain injury six months ago and is recovering in her family's home far from me. I'm studying history full-time. I use a shared calendar for her rehab appointments and a WhatsApp group with her mum, but I feel like I'm always the one chasing for updates and I don't know if I'm being overbearing or appropriately involved.

That tension, wanting to stay informed versus fearing you're pushing too hard, is something a lot of long-distance caregiving partners feel, and it doesn't get talked about enough. A couple of things to think about: have you asked her mum what kind of update cadence would work for her, weekly, or after each appointment? Sometimes naming it directly removes the guesswork. And what does your girlfriend herself want from you in terms of involvement? If she can tell you, her preference is the one that matters most, and it might relieve the pressure you're putting on yourself.

My older brother has dementia and I've been his distance carer from Poland for three years now. I work full-time in social work and on bad weeks I just go numb. I can't feel anything at work or at home. People at the temple notice and ask if I'm okay and I just say yes because I don't know what else to say.

Going numb when you're stretched thin isn't a failure of feeling. It's your mind rationing energy when there's been too much for too long. Three years of distance care alongside full-time social work is enormous. Two practical things: when someone at temple asks, try 'Honestly, it's been a heavy few weeks'. You don't have to explain more, and it lets people in. And that numbness is worth mentioning to your GP, especially if it's lasting days or weeks at a stretch. It's a signal, not a personality change.

My cousin in another city has early-onset Alzheimer's and I've cared from Sweden for two years. I'm studying economics and working part-time, and lately I get angry at small things and then cry for no reason. I feel like I'm cracking and I don't know if it's the caregiving or just me.

That cracking feeling, the sudden anger, the unexpected tears, is a very common response to sustained caregiving pressure, especially when you're balancing study and work too. It's not 'just you' breaking. It's your system overloaded. Two things: track those moments for a week (what triggered them, when), patterns often emerge that point to specific things you can adjust. And please talk to your university's student health service or your GP about what you're feeling. What you're describing is your mind asking for support, not a sign of weakness.

My girlfriend has epilepsy and I've supported her from the UK for three years. I'm studying biology at college and trying to hold to Hindu values of duty. But every time she has a seizure and I'm not there I spiral for days. I can't eat, can't study. I feel like duty is eating me alive.

My grandmother's early-onset Alzheimer's has progressed over two years. I'm in Brazil working full-time in history, she's elsewhere. I manage her household remotely, bills, staff, medical scheduling. My own work keeps slipping and I'm exhausted. I can't keep doing both at this level.

Running someone's entire household remotely alongside a full-time job is a huge load, and it makes complete sense that your work is slipping, something has to give. Two steps: list every recurring task and flag which ones could be delegated to a local person, a neighbour, a paid care manager, or a relative who hasn't been carrying any of this. Then take that list to your manager and ask about temporary flexible hours or reduced load. Many workplaces can accommodate this for a set period. You don't have to do everything at the same level forever. This is a phase to get through, not a permanent arrangement.

My grandmother in Suriname has had early-onset Alzheimer's for three years. I coordinate her care from here in the Netherlands while studying biology. Lately I feel this deep sadness that comes in waves. I'll be fine, then suddenly I'm crying in the library. It's embarrassing.

Those waves of grief are a natural response to losing someone gradually. You're mourning someone who's still alive, and it doesn't announce itself on a schedule. Crying in the library isn't embarrassing. It's your grief finding the only gap it could. A couple of things: see if your university has a counsellor you can speak to regularly, someone who can hold space for that sadness rather than you managing it alone between study sessions. And if you practice prayer or meditation as part of your faith, some people find that ritual helps them sit with grief rather than fight it. The waves may not stop, but you don't have to drown in them alone.

My Hindu faith teaches me devotion but honestly watching him decline so slowly is its own kind of grief. Every day he's a little less himself and I don't know how to mourn someone who's still here.

Contact a Parkinson's support organisation, many run groups specifically for partners, and being with people who understand that slow grief can be deeply grounding. Also consider speaking to a counsellor who works with carers, mourning in a healthy way while still showing up daily is a skill, and you shouldn't have to figure it out alone.

A overflowing medical folder is a common problem. It grows faster than you organise it. Try creating subfolders by category, scans, lab results, appointment summaries, medication lists, and rename files with dates in the format YYYY-MM-DD so they sort automatically. Most phones let you search within folders, so consistent naming makes a huge difference. If her hospital offers a patient portal, check whether you can access records there instead. It might already be organised and updated without you doing anything. And ask her oncology team if they need copies or can access her records directly, which might reduce what you need to carry.

I'm 25, no religion, Indigenous, recently graduated in engineering in the Philippines. My aunt has dementia and I've been her distance carer for two years. She's started telling me elaborate stories about things that never happened and gets angry when I correct her. I don't want to lie to her but the truth upsets her.

This is one of the most common and difficult dementia dilemmas, and the answer from dementia specialists is usually: stop correcting. Her stories aren't lies to her. They're her brain's current reality, and correcting them causes distress without any benefit. Try joining her reality instead: 'That sounds like quite a day, tell me more about it.' You're not lying, you're meeting her where she is. Dementia organisations have excellent guides on this approach, often called validation therapy, and her care team can help you practice it. Two years of distance caregiving is a lot, please look into support for yourself too.
